title: How to face swap a long video, shot by shot
summary: Face swap one person across an edited video. Keep the original timeline, match the same identity across cuts, and fix only the shots that fail.
body_markdown:
If one person needs a new face across a long edited video, keep the original timeline and work on the shots where that person is visible. Use one replacement identity throughout, check the target face again after each cut, and compare adjacent shots before exporting. Leave reaction shots and cutaways alone unless they also need the change.


## Choose the shots you actually need to change


Duplicate your timeline before exporting anything. Mark the shots where the target’s face is visible and where changing it matters. Leave a shot out if the person is offscreen, their face is too small to identify, or the edit works with a cutaway. If the brief also changes hair, wardrobe or the body, use the[actor replacement workflow](https://magichour.ai/blog/how-to-replace-an-actor-in-a-video-without-reshooting) .


Keep the original audio, captions, cut points and source files on the editing timeline. Export just the picture segments you plan to process. If the edit still needs transitions or extended handles, leave that extra footage on each end so you have room to trim the replacement back into the cut.


## Approve one shot before you process the rest


Start with a shot that represents the difficulty of the project. A close-up that includes the head turn you’re worried about tells you more than a perfectly still opening frame. Use a sharp, evenly lit photo with one visible face. Keep that photo as the default across shots. If an angle genuinely calls for another reference, use an image of the same person and compare the result against the first approved shot.


Open[Magic Hour Video Face Swap](https://magichour.ai/products/face-swap/video) and check the time range, face selection and estimate before submitting. When another person is in frame, use a selection that targets the intended person and confirm the mapping in that shot. The[Face Swap guide](https://help.magichour.ai/en/articles/12614442-how-to-swap-a-face-from-a-photo-into-a-video) explains how to pick specific faces. Magic Hour’s[troubleshooting guide](https://help.magichour.ai/en/articles/15011100-face-swap-video-troubleshooting) recommends trying Smart face handling for turns and temporary obstructions where that option is available.


## Go back over the cuts with sound on


Put each approved clip over its original shot. Play through the cut from both directions and inspect the first and last frames of each replacement. Check that the right person changes, the identity holds across angles, and hands or glasses still sit in front of the face when they should. Listen for any shift in the words or rhythm against the picture.


If the identity changes at one cut, keep the shots that passed and reopen the failing shot. Double-check its mapping, crop or reference angle before paying for another attempt. A brief cutaway can solve an obstructed shot when matching the original image matters less than keeping the scene readable.


## What the tool walkthrough shows


[Watch the walkthrough on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I5RdUDfuC_A) .


This Magic Hour walkthrough shows the inputs for one clip. The editing steps above cover how to use those same inputs and checks on a timeline with several shots.


## What to price before buying credits


Add up the durations of the shots you’ll process, then check the tool’s quote for those selections and leave room for revisions. A short preview tells you whether the face works at that angle and whether the exported clip fits your edit. Compare[video face-swap app limits and costs](https://magichour.ai/blog/best-face-swap-video-apps) if you need a different clip length, local processing or another export format.


Get permission for the footage and the replacement likeness before starting, and follow your platform’s disclosure rules where they apply. When the first shot passes, keep its reference and settings beside your edit so you can reproduce them on the next shot.
